newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hashimoto faces hard choices in naming new cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto faces hard choices in naming new cabinet.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, set to be re-elected when parliament reconvenes on Thursday, faces the daunting task of naming a new cabinet that would show how serious he is about promised reforms.
Hashimoto is certain to win the majority of votes in the new 500-seat Lower House on the strength of a loose alliance his party formed last week with the Social Democrats and the tiny Sakigake party.

But Hashimoto in effect will lead a minority government because his Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) first failed to win a Lower House majority on its own in general elections held last month and then failed to renew a straightforward coalition with its two allies.
That means Hashimoto's new 20-member cabinet would be an all-LDP team, for the first time since 1993.

The Lower House of Japan's parliament is given constitutional precedence over the Upper House in naming the prime minister, enacting budget bills and ratifying treaties. The prime minister must be a member of the Lower House.

In his new cabinet to be formed Thursday evening, Hashimoto will retain his foreign minister, Yukihiko Ikeda, because of a busy foreign policy schedule, including key talks with the United States, Russia and China, ministry sources said.
Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov arrives in Tokyo on November 14 to resume talks over the vexed question of Russian-held islands claimed by Japan.
The dispute over the islands, called the Southern Kuriles by Moscow and the Northern Territories by Tokyo, has kept the two countries from signing a World War Two peace treaty.

The following week in Manila during an Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum ministerial meeting, Ikeda was also expected to hold talks with U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.

Hashimoto has also decided to keep LDP stalwart Seiroku Kajiyama as chief cabinet secretary, who performs the twin role of cabinet coordinator and official government spokesman, parliamentary sources said.

By far the most important appointment in the new cabinet will be the finance portfolio, to be vacated by outgoing Social Democrat Wataru Kubo. It will be a hard act to follow because Kubo has been credited with skilfully handling a powerful ministry besieged by public outrage and now the prime target of Hashimoto's promised reforms.

The public outcry stemmed from scandals involving the ministry's top bureaucrats and an unpopular plan that used tax money to pay for the ministry's mismanagement of banks and other financial institutions.
A likely candidate for the office is Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, a former trade minister and leader of one of the intra-party factions that make up the LDP.

But it remained to be seen whether Mitsuzuka, a member of the LDP's old guard, can preside over a break up of the ministry, centreing on the planned separation of the department overseeing banks and other financial institutions.

Last week, Hashimoto's tripartite alliance drafted a policy document which pledged to introduce a Finance Ministry reform bill along those lines during the regular 150-day session of parliament to start in January.
Opposition party members said they were closely watching who would be named as construction, transport, trade, and farm ministers -- posts traditionally associated with the LDP's vested interests.

If Hashimoto appoints members of the LDP's old guard to those posts, this could endanger his promised government reforms. On the other hand, he cannot risk alienating them since they were instrumental in his election as LDP president.
